<h1>Group B — Contraception dataset</h1>

<p><strong>What this study is:</strong> a <em>cross-sectional</em> study — one sample
per person, taken at a single time point (not before/after, unlike Group A).
It asks how three contraceptive methods relate to the vaginal microbiome,
host gene expression, and inflammation.</p>

<h2>The study design</h2>

<p><strong>93 participants</strong>, one vaginal sample each, in three arms:</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Arm (contraceptive method)</th><th>Number of people (n)</th></tr>
  <tr><td>injectable (e.g. DMPA injection)</td><td>39</td></tr>
  <tr><td>pill (oral contraceptive)</td><td>28</td></tr>
  <tr><td>vaginal ring</td><td>26</td></tr>
  <tr><td><strong>Total</strong></td><td><strong>93</strong></td></tr>
</table>

<h2>The six files</h2>

<table class="files">
  <tr><th>File</th><th>Size</th><th>What it holds</th></tr>
  <tr><td>01_metadata.csv</td><td>93 rows</td><td>One row per participant — who they are and their clinical info</td></tr>
  <tr><td>02_microbiome_counts.csv</td><td>220 × 93</td><td>Bacterial species (rows) × samples (columns); raw read counts</td></tr>
  <tr><td>03_microbiome_taxonomy.csv</td><td>220 rows</td><td>Name lookup for the species table: Domain → Phylum → … → species</td></tr>
  <tr><td>04_rnaseq_counts.csv.gz</td><td>14,226 × 93</td><td>Human genes (rows) × samples (columns); raw RNA-seq read counts</td></tr>
  <tr><td>05_gene_annotation.csv</td><td>14,226 rows</td><td>Name lookup for the gene table: Ensembl ID, symbol, gene name, type</td></tr>
  <tr><td>06_cytokines.csv</td><td>93 × 15</td><td>Concentrations of 15 immune signalling proteins per sample</td></tr>
</table>

<p>Both count tables are <strong>features in rows, samples in columns</strong>.
The <code>.gz</code> on the gene file just means it is compressed — R reads it
without you doing anything special.</p>

<h2>Metadata column meanings</h2>

<table>
  <tr><th>Column</th><th>What it means</th></tr>
  <tr><td><code>sample_id</code></td><td>Unique sample code (B001, B002, …)</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>participant_id</code></td><td>Which person the sample came from. Same as sample_id here, because each person gave one sample</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>arm</code></td><td>Contraceptive method: <code>pill</code>, <code>injectable</code>, or <code>ring</code>. <strong>The main grouping variable</strong></td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>bv</code></td><td>Bacterial vaginosis status: <code>negative</code> (51), <code>positive</code> (39), <code>intermediate</code> (3)</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>nugent</code></td><td>Nugent score, 0–10, from examining bacteria under a microscope. Higher = more BV-like</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>ph</code></td><td>Vaginal pH. Healthy is typically below ~4.5; higher suggests disturbed flora / BV</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>any_sti</code></td><td>Any sexually transmitted infection present (1 = yes, 48 people; 0 = no, 45)</td></tr>
  <tr><td><code>rnaseq_batch</code></td><td>Lab processing batch (<code>B1</code> = 47, <code>B2</code> = 46). Batch effects can masquerade as real differences — worth checking</td></tr>
</table>

<h2>The cytokines (06_cytokines.csv)</h2>

<p>15 immune signalling proteins measured from the same samples:
<code>il1b</code>, <code>il6</code>, <code>tnfa</code>, <code>ifny</code>,
<code>il10</code>, <code>il4</code>, <code>il17a</code>, <code>il17f</code>,
<code>il21</code>, <code>il22</code>, <code>il23</code>, <code>il25</code>,
<code>il31</code>, <code>il33</code>, <code>scd40l</code>.</p>

<p>These are continuous concentration values, <em>not</em> counts. They are the
readout of <strong>inflammation</strong> — e.g. does a microbiome pattern seen
across arms come with an inflammatory shift?</p>

<h2>The two big rules for this week</h2>

<ol>
  <li><strong>Raw counts go into DESeq2.</strong> Never CPM, never pre-logged —
  DESeq2 does its own normalisation.</li>
  <li><strong>Do not define a group from one count table and test that same
  table.</strong> Define the group from the metadata (e.g. <code>arm</code> or
  <code>bv</code>), then test the species table <em>or</em> the gene table.</li>
</ol>

<div class="note">
<p><strong>Also keep in mind:</strong> both count tables are compositional —
"relative abundance went down" is not the same claim as "there was less of it".</p>
</div>

<h2>Project question: does the microbiome differ by contraceptive arm?</h2>

<p>Below, the data answer this in four steps: (1) is sequencing depth comparable
across arms, (2) does <em>diversity within</em> a sample differ, (3) does the
<em>whole community</em> differ, and (4) <em>which species</em> drive any difference.
All figures and numbers come from the R script
<code>group_project/analysis-microbiome-arm.R</code>.</p>

<h3>Step 0 — are the arms comparable to begin with?</h3>

<p>Before any test: sequencing depth ("library size", reads per sample) should
be similar across arms, otherwise differences could just reflect how deeply
each sample was sequenced. They are:</p>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Boxplot of library size by arm" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> one box per contraceptive arm, showing
how many sequencing reads each participant's sample received (dots are
individual participants). Equal-height boxes mean no arm was sequenced more
deeply than another.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> the boxes sit at the same height (median ≈
29,000 reads everywhere). Sequencing depth is comparable, so any differences
we find later are unlikely to be an artefact of how deeply samples were
sequenced.</p>
</div>

<h3>Step 1 — diversity within a sample (alpha diversity)</h3>

<p>Shannon diversity asks: within one sample, how many species are present and
how evenly are they spread? A Lactobacillus-dominated sample scores low; a
diverse BV-like community scores high.</p>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Boxplot of Shannon diversity by arm" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<table>
  <tr><th>Arm</th><th>Median Shannon</th><th>IQR (middle 50%)</th></tr>
  <tr><td>pill</td><td>0.90</td><td>0.58 – 1.81</td></tr>
  <tr><td>injectable</td><td>1.74</td><td>0.59 – 2.32</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ring</td><td>1.59</td><td>0.49 – 2.18</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> each box is the Shannon diversity of
one arm's participants — low values = a few species dominating (e.g. a
Lactobacillus-dominated sample), high values = many species coexisting. The
table gives the medians and the middle 50% of each arm. A significant
Kruskal–Wallis test would mean the arms' typical diversity differs.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> no clear difference. The boxes overlap
heavily and the test is non-significant (p = 0.47; all pairwise adjusted
p ≥ 0.61). The spread <em>within</em> each arm is huge — some pill users also
have diverse communities — so the method does not set a participant's diversity.</p>
</div>

<h3>Step 2 — what the communities are made of</h3>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Stacked bars of mean relative abundance of top genera by arm" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<p>Lactobacillus dominates all three arms on average, but less so in the
injectable and ring arms, which show more anaerobic bacteria (Gardnerella,
Prevotella, Sneathia — taxa associated with BV). Counting samples that are
<em>Lactobacillus-dominant</em> (&gt;50% of reads):</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Arm</th><th>Lactobacillus-dominant samples</th><th>Share of arm</th><th>Mean Lactobacillus share</th></tr>
  <tr><td>pill</td><td>17 of 28</td><td>61%</td><td>59%</td></tr>
  <tr><td>injectable</td><td>19 of 39</td><td>49%</td><td>49%</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ring</td><td>12 of 26</td><td>46%</td><td>51%</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing (fig3 + table):</strong> the stacked bars are
each arm's <em>average</em> community — each coloured segment is one genus's
average share of reads, so taller green = more Lactobacillus on average. The
table turns it into a head-count: how many participants in each arm have a
Lactobacillus-dominated sample (over half of reads).</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> every arm is Lactobacillus-dominated on
average, but less so moving from pill (61% of samples dominant) to injectable
(49%) and ring (46%) — those two arms show more anaerobic bacteria
(Gardnerella, Prevotella, Sneathia), the taxa associated with BV.</p>
</div>

<p class="note">Remember the compositional caveat: these are <em>shares of
reads</em>. "Less Lactobacillus" here means a smaller slice of the pie, not
proof that there were fewer Lactobacillus cells.</p>

<h3>Step 3 — does the whole community differ? (beta diversity)</h3>

<p>Each point below is one participant's full community (Bray–Curtis
ordination, a PCoA). Points that sit close together have similar communities.</p>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="PCoA of Bray-Curtis distances coloured by arm" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<p>The arms overlap substantially. A PERMANOVA (a permutation test asking
"do the groups differ in community composition?") gives:</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Model</th><th>R² (variation explained)</th><th>p-value</th></tr>
  <tr><td>arm + bv + any_sti + batch</td><td>0.27</td><td>0.001</td></tr>
  <tr><td>arm on its own</td><td>0.03</td><td>≈ 0.1 (borderline, not significant)</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing (fig4 + table):</strong> each point is one
participant's whole community placed by how similar it is to the others —
nearby points have similar communities. If an arm genuinely shaped the
microbiome, its colour would clump together. The table's R² is the share of
that clustering pattern the variable explains, and the p-value asks whether it
is more than chance.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> the three colours intermingle. Arm alone
explains only ~3% of community variation (R² = 0.03, p ≈ 0.1, not clearly
significant), while the full model with BV, STI and batch reaches R² = 0.27
(p = 0.001) — so the strong drivers here are BV status and the covariates,
not the contraceptive method.</p>
</div>

<h3>Step 4 — which species differ? (DESeq2 on raw counts)</h3>

<p>DESeq2 was run on <strong>raw counts</strong> with the design
<code>~ rnaseq_batch + bv + arm</code> (adjusting for batch and BV status so we
pick out arm differences, not those). 110 of 220 species were kept after a
minimal filter (total reads ≥ 10).</p>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Log2 fold changes of top species, injectable vs pill" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Log2 fold changes of top species, ring vs pill" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> each bar is one significant species,
and its length is how much more (right, orange) or less (left, blue) of it a
participant has in the first arm of the pair compared with the second. Longer
bars and smaller adjusted p-values = more confident differences.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> ring vs pill has the most differences (27
species vs 6 for injectable vs pill), and the pattern is one-directional:
BV-associated anaerobes (<em>Atopobium</em>, <em>Mobiluncus</em>,
<em>Prevotella</em>) are enriched in ring users, while pill users lean towards
Lactobacillus-dominance.</p>
</div>

<table>
  <tr><th>Contrast</th><th>Species significant at adjusted p &lt; 0.05</th></tr>
  <tr><td>injectable vs pill</td><td>6</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ring vs pill</td><td>27</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ring vs injectable</td><td>14</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> a head-count of how many species
passed the significance test in each pairwise comparison — the total volume of
species-level difference between each pair of arms.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> the ring is the most distinct arm (27 species
vs pill, 14 vs injectable); the pill and injectable arms differ the least
(6 species). Even the biggest number is only 27 of 220 species — a small
fraction of the community.</p>
</div>

<p>Top hits (positive log2FC = higher in the first arm of the pair):</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Contrast</th><th>Species</th><th>log2FC</th><th>adjusted p</th><th>Direction</th></tr>
  <tr><td rowspan="4">injectable vs pill</td><td><em>Mageeibacillus indolicus</em></td><td>+10.0</td><td>8.2e−08</td><td>more in injectable</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>Sneathia amnii</em></td><td>+4.2</td><td>6.3e−04</td><td>more in injectable</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>Prevotella</em> sp. 1</td><td>+5.4</td><td>9.0e−03</td><td>more in injectable</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>Lactobacillus crispatus</em></td><td>+2.0</td><td>6.3e−03</td><td>more in injectable*</td></tr>
  <tr><td rowspan="5">ring vs pill</td><td><em>Atopobium minutum</em></td><td>+28.3</td><td>1.4e−11</td><td>more in ring</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>Mobiluncus curtisii</em></td><td>+11.7</td><td>7.4e−07</td><td>more in ring</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>Prevotella timonensis</em></td><td>+4.7</td><td>3.4e−06</td><td>more in ring</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>Dialister</em> sp.</td><td>+5.2</td><td>3.4e−05</td><td>more in ring</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>Corynebacterium glucuronolyticum</em></td><td>−21.6</td><td>5.2e−07</td><td>more in pill</td></tr>
</table>

<p style="font-size:.9em">* <em>L. crispatus</em> being higher in the injectable
arm despite its lower overall Lactobacillus share is a good reminder that a
mean share (step 2) and a per-species DESeq2 test answer slightly different
questions — worth discussing in your write-up.</p>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> each row is one species that passed the
significance test; log2FC is the size of the difference (doubling per +1) and
“Direction” says which arm has more of it.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> the species that do differ are almost all
BV-associated anaerobes, higher in ring and injectable users
(<em>Mageeibacillus</em>, <em>Sneathia</em>, <em>Prevotella</em>,
<em>Atopobium</em>, <em>Mobiluncus</em>); the exception worth flagging is
<em>L. crispatus</em>, slightly higher in the injectable arm.</p>
</div>

<h3>Overall answer</h3>

<div class="note">
<p><strong>Differences between contraceptive arms are modest.</strong> Alpha
diversity does not differ (p = 0.47); community composition differs only
weakly if at all by arm (R² ≈ 0.03, p ≈ 0.1) once you account for how much BV
status dominates. Where DESeq2 does find species-level differences, the
pattern is consistent: ring users (and to a lesser degree injectable users)
harbour more BV-associated anaerobes (<em>Atopobium</em>, <em>Mobiluncus</em>,
<em>Prevotella</em>, <em>Sneathia</em>), while pill users lean more
Lactobacillus-dominant. A follow-up worth proposing: test <code>bv</code> as the
main variable — it is likely the much stronger signal in this dataset.</p>
</div>

<h2>Project question: does the ring differ from the systemic methods in host gene expression?</h2>

<p>The ring delivers hormone <em>locally</em> at the vagina; the pill and the
injectable act <em>systemically</em>. So the analysis defines a new variable
from the metadata (never from the counts being tested):</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Route</th><th>Members</th><th>n</th></tr>
  <tr><td><strong>local</strong></td><td>ring</td><td>26</td></tr>
  <tr><td><strong>systemic</strong></td><td>pill + injectable</td><td>67 (28 + 39)</td></tr>
</table>

<p>All figures come from the R script <code>group_project/analysis-genes-ring.R</code>,
which tests the <strong>gene table</strong> (14,226 human genes, raw counts into
DESeq2).</p>

<h3>Step 0 — comparable sequencing depth?</h3>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Boxplot of RNA-seq library size by route" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> the same sequencing-depth check as
fig1, but for the RNA-seq gene table, with samples grouped by delivery route
(green = ring/local, blue = pill + injectable/systemic). Equal boxes mean both
routes were sequenced equally deeply.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> near-identical depth (medians ≈ 12.8M local
vs 13.0M mapped reads). Gene-expression differences later are not a sequencing-
depth artefact.</p>
</div>

<h3>Step 1 — the big picture: do ring samples separate?</h3>

<p>PCA on the 500 most variable genes (variance-stabilised values — a transform
used <em>only for this plot</em>; the test below uses raw counts). Each point is
one participant.</p>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="PCA of gene expression coloured by route" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> each point is one participant's entire
gene-expression profile, squeezed into two dimensions so similar profiles sit
close together. Green squares = ring users; blue circles/triangles = the two
systemic arms. A real local-vs-systemic effect would push the green squares
away from the blue cloud.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> there <em>is</em> a visible shift — ring
samples drift right along PC1 (mean +4.6 vs −1.8) — but with substantial
overlap, not two clean clusters. Expect a real but modest molecular signal.</p>
</div>

<h3>Step 2 — formal test: DESeq2 on raw counts</h3>

<p>Design: <code>~ rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti + route</code> — adjusting for
lab batch, BV status and STI status, so route is not confused with them.
Genes with fewer than 10 total reads were dropped (keeps most of the 14,226).</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Result (local vs systemic)</th><th>Count</th></tr>
  <tr><td>Genes tested</td><td>14,226</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Significant at adjusted p &lt; 0.05</td><td><strong>66</strong> (0.5%)</td></tr>
  <tr><td>&nbsp;&nbsp;— higher in ring (local)</td><td>40</td></tr>
  <tr><td>&nbsp;&nbsp;— higher in systemic methods</td><td>26</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> a head-count of DESeq2's verdict on
every gene: does expression differ between ring users and the systemic
methods, after adjusting for batch, BV and STI? Only genes surviving the
multiple-testing correction count.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> yes, but subtly — 66 of 14,226 genes (0.5%)
differ: 40 higher in ring, 26 higher in systemic. A real, focused signal,
not a wholesale rewrite of the tissue's biology.</p>
</div>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Log2 fold changes of top genes, ring vs systemic" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<p>Top genes higher in ring users:</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Gene</th><th>What it does</th><th>log2FC</th><th>adjusted p</th></tr>
  <tr><td><em>BPIFA1</em></td><td>an antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory protein secreted at wet epithelial surfaces</td><td>+5.8</td><td>4.2e−11</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>PTGS2</em> (COX-2)</td><td>the key enzyme making inflammatory prostaglandins</td><td>+1.6</td><td>3.4e−03</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>ACOD1</em></td><td>an immune-response gene (part of the interferon reaction)</td><td>+2.8</td><td>8.7e−03</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>SERPINA11</em>, <em>CHGA</em>, <em>KDR</em>, <em>PLXNA4</em></td><td>secreted/membrane proteins (less familiar in this tissue)</td><td>+1.7 to +3.9</td><td>2.4e−03 to 2.9e−05</td></tr>
</table>

<p>Top genes higher in the systemic methods (pill + injectable):</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Gene</th><th>What it does</th><th>log2FC</th><th>adjusted p</th></tr>
  <tr><td><em>TGM3</em></td><td>cross-links proteins during squamous epithelial maturation</td><td>−3.7</td><td>3.8e−07</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>KPRP</em></td><td>a keratinocyte structural protein</td><td>−3.4</td><td>9.2e−05</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>KRT1</em></td><td>keratin 1 — a hallmark of squamous epithelium</td><td>−2.3</td><td>6.2e−04</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>EPN3</em>, <em>UPK3B</em>, <em>CEACAM7</em>, <em>FBLN2</em></td><td>epithelial/structural genes</td><td>−1.3 to −1.9</td><td>1.9e−03 to 5.4e−03</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing (fig8 + tables):</strong> the bar chart shows the
biggest gene-expression differences (orange = higher in ring, blue = higher in
systemic); the tables name the top genes in each direction and what they do.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> the two gene programmes are biologically
coherent. Ring samples lean towards secretory and inflammatory genes
(<em>BPIFA1</em>, an antimicrobial protein; <em>PTGS2</em>/COX-2;
<em>ACOD1</em>, interferon response), while systemic-method samples lean
towards squamous-epithelial maturation genes (<em>TGM3</em>, <em>KPRP</em>,
<em>KRT1</em>). The ring tissue reads as slightly inflamed and secretory.</p>
</div>

<h3>Step 3 — consistency check</h3>

<p>If the local-vs-systemic signal is real, ring should differ from <em>both</em>
systemic methods in the same direction (separate model with
<code>arm</code> in the design):</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Contrast</th><th>Significant genes</th></tr>
  <tr><td>ring vs pill</td><td>60</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ring vs injectable</td><td>87</td></tr>
  <tr><td>significant in <em>both</em></td><td>11 — and all 11 point the same direction</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> a test of the route logic. If “local
vs systemic” is the real story, ring should differ from the pill AND from the
injectable in the same direction; the table counts significant genes per
contrast and their overlap.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> all 11 genes significant in both contrasts
point the same direction, which supports the story — but only 11 of 66 are
shared, so much of the signal is contrast-specific (and ring-vs-injectable,
87 genes, is the strongest pair, matching the microbiome result).</p>
</div>

<div class="note">
<p><strong>Overall answer: yes, modestly but consistently.</strong> About 0.5%
of genes differ between ring and the systemic methods, and the two
programmes they point to are biologically coherent: ring samples show higher
expression of <strong>secretory and inflammatory genes</strong>
(<em>BPIFA1</em>, <em>PTGS2</em>, <em>ACOD1</em>), while systemic-method samples
show higher <strong>squamous-epithelial maturation genes</strong>
(<em>TGM3</em>, <em>KPRP</em>, <em>KRT1</em>). One caution for your write-up:
<em>BPIFA1</em> is induced by bacterial exposure, and the ring arm also had the
most BV-associated microbiome — so some of the host signal may be the tissue
responding to its microbes rather than a direct hormonal effect. Adjusting for
clinical BV status helps, but does not fully untangle this.</p>
</div>

<h3>How to check this analysis yourself</h3>

<pre><code>Rscript group_project/analysis-genes-ring.R</code></pre>

<p>Sanity checks that would catch a mistake:</p>
<ul>
  <li>The route table should print 26 ring (local) and 67 systemic (28 + 39).</li>
  <li>In fig7, green squares should sit slightly right of blue circles/triangles — matching mean PC1 +4.6 vs −1.8, but with overlap (so no test should claim a dramatic separation).</li>
  <li><em>BPIFA1</em> is the single most significant gene (adjusted p = 4.2e−11) and has a large positive log2FC. You can spot-check it directly:</li>
</ul>

<pre><code>d &lt;- read_counts("group_b")
row &lt;- d$gene_info |&gt; dplyr::filter(symbol == "BPIFA1") |&gt; dplyr::pull(ensembl_gene_id)
barplot(d$genes[row, ] / 1e3, col = ifelse(d$metadata$arm == "ring", "green", "grey"),
        las = 2, ylab = "BPIFA1 reads (thousands)")</code></pre>

<p>If the page is right, green (ring) bars should generally be taller.</p>

<h2>Project question: community type vs method — which explains genes better?</h2>

<p>Instead of grouping people by contraceptive method, we group them by
<strong>community type</strong> — clusters of similar vaginal microbiomes, the
classic “community state types” — defined from the <strong>species count
table</strong>, then test the <strong>gene table</strong>. This respects the
workshop rule: the group is defined from one table, and the other table is what
we test.</p>

<h3>Step 1 — define community types from the microbiome</h3>

<p>Method in plain words: we measure how similar every pair of participants'
microbiomes are (Bray–Curtis distance), then cluster them (Ward's method) and
cut the tree into 3 groups — the number of clusters chosen because it had the
best silhouette score (a measure of clustering quality) among 2, 3, 4 and 5:</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Number of clusters tried (k)</th><th>2</th><th>3 (chosen)</th><th>4</th><th>5</th></tr>
  <tr><td>mean silhouette</td><td>0.245</td><td><strong>0.323</strong></td><td>0.314</td><td>0.311</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> a cluster-quality score (silhouette)
for each candidate number of groups, from 2 to 5. Higher = samples fit their
assigned group better and the groups are better separated.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> k = 3 scores best (0.323), though only
moderately — the community types are real but blend into each other at the
edges, so treat them as useful categories, not crisp boxes.</p>
</div>

<p>The three clusters have clear biological identities:</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Community type</th><th>n</th><th>Shannon (microbiome)</th><th>mean <em>L. crispatus</em> share</th><th>mean Gardnerella share</th></tr>
  <tr><td>C3 — <em>L. crispatus</em>-dominant</td><td>21</td><td>0.49</td><td>84%</td><td>0.2%</td></tr>
  <tr><td>C1 — <em>L. iners</em>-dominant</td><td>24</td><td>0.77</td><td>8%</td><td>1.7%</td></tr>
  <tr><td>C2 — Diverse (BV-like)</td><td>48</td><td>2.05</td><td>3%</td><td>5.9%</td></tr>
</table>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Stacked bars of mean composition by community type" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing (table + fig10):</strong> the table characterises
each cluster (how many people, how diverse, which Lactobacillus species
dominates); fig10 shows each type's average community. Remember these are
definitions, not tests — the clusters were built from this table.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> three textbook vaginal types: two
Lactobacillus-dominated ones split by <em>which</em> species
(<em>L. crispatus</em>, n=21, lowest diversity; <em>L. iners</em>, n=24), and a
large diverse/BV-like type (n=48) full of Gardnerella, Prevotella and
Sneathia.</p>
</div>

<p>How do the types relate to method and to BV? They overlap, but are not the
same thing:</p>

<table>
  <tr><th></th><th>C3 crispatus-dom</th><th>C1 iners-dom</th><th>C2 diverse</th></tr>
  <tr><td>pill (28)</td><td>4</td><td>12</td><td>12</td></tr>
  <tr><td>injectable (39)</td><td>12</td><td>3</td><td>24</td></tr>
  <tr><td>ring (26)</td><td>5</td><td>9</td><td>12</td></tr>
</table>

<table>
  <tr><th></th><th>C3 crispatus-dom</th><th>C1 iners-dom</th><th>C2 diverse</th></tr>
  <tr><td>BV negative (51)</td><td>20</td><td>22</td><td>9</td></tr>
  <tr><td>BV positive (39)</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>37</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> two cross-counts of the same 93
participants: which contraceptive arm each community type falls into, and which
BV status.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> community type tracks BV far more tightly
than it tracks method: 37 of 39 BV-positive participants sit in the diverse
type, while the type–method spread is only partial (injectable leans diverse,
24 of 39; pill splits 12/12 between iners-dom and diverse). Community type and
contraceptive method are related but not the same variable — exactly what the
gene comparison below needs.</p>
</div>

<h3>Step 2 — test the genes: which grouping explains more?</h3>

<p>Two different ways to compare, because “explains more” can mean two things:</p>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Per-gene count:</strong> a DESeq2 likelihood-ratio test (LRT) asks,
  gene by gene, “does adding this grouping variable to the design improve the
  fit for this gene?” We count genes where it does (adjusted p &lt; 0.05).
  Both groupings get the same design otherwise:
  <code>~ rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti + grouping</code>. (Important: we adjust
  for BV, since the diverse type is nearly all BV-positive — otherwise the
  comparison would mostly re-discover BV.)</li>
  <li><strong>Genome-wide variance:</strong> a PERMANOVA on the gene expression
  profiles (variance-stabilised values of the 2,000 most variable genes,
  Euclidean distances) asks how much of the <em>overall</em> variation each
  grouping explains (R²).</li>
</ul>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Bar chart of significant gene counts by grouping variable" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<table>
  <tr><th>Grouping</th><th>Significant genes (adjusted p &lt; 0.05)</th></tr>
  <tr><td>community type (3 levels)</td><td><strong>93</strong></td></tr>
  <tr><td>arm — pill/injectable/ring (3 levels)</td><td>49</td></tr>
  <tr><td>route — local vs systemic (2 levels, from previous section)</td><td>66</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing (fig11 + table):</strong> one bar per grouping
variable, counting how many host genes change when that variable is added to
the DESeq2 model (adjusted p &lt; 0.05). Taller bar = the grouping explains
more individual genes. All three models adjust for the same covariates
(batch, BV, STI), so the comparison is fair.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> community type explains more genes than
method does — 93 vs 49 (route: 66). The microbiome state is a better pointer
to specific host genes than the contraceptive method is.</p>
</div>

<p>Top community-type genes (LRT has no single effect size; the numbers
are mean expression per type on the variance-stabilised scale):</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Gene</th><th>Known for</th><th>adj. p</th><th>crispatus-dom</th><th>iners-dom</th><th>diverse</th></tr>
  <tr><td><em>ARL4C</em></td><td>small GTPase, cell shape/migration</td><td>0.0015</td><td>8.8</td><td>7.9</td><td>8.0</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>EDN2</em></td><td>endothelin 2, epithelial peptide</td><td>0.0056</td><td>7.1</td><td>6.2</td><td>5.9</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>CCNG2</em></td><td>cell-cycle braking (cyclin G2)</td><td>0.0280</td><td>10.9</td><td>10.5</td><td>10.2</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>EPG5</em></td><td>autophagy regulator</td><td>0.0023</td><td>10.5</td><td>10.1</td><td>10.0</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>HDAC4</em></td><td>chromatin modifier</td><td>0.0290</td><td>8.7</td><td>8.9</td><td>8.9</td></tr>
  <tr><td><em>WEE1</em></td><td>cell-cycle checkpoint kinase</td><td>0.0290</td><td>8.3</td><td>8.6</td><td>8.1</td></tr>
</table>

<p style="font-size:.9em">Full results: <code>group_project/results/deseq2_lrt_ctype.csv</code>.
Note the honest pattern: most top genes are <em>highest</em> in the
crispatus-dominant type and lowest in the diverse type, but the differences are
small (≈ 0.5–1.2 on this scale) — these are subtle shifts, and the top genes
are cell-cycle/epithelial genes rather than a dramatic immune story.</p>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing:</strong> the strongest community-type genes;
the three number columns are each type's average expression of that gene
(higher = more active). A clear pattern would be one type standing apart.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> most top genes (e.g. <em>ARL4C</em>,
<em>EDN2</em>, <em>CCNG2</em>) are highest in the crispatus-dominant type and
lowest in the diverse type, but the gaps are small (≈ 0.5–1.2) and the genes
are cell-cycle/epithelial rather than an immune story — consistent with a
healthier, less disturbed tissue in Lactobacillus-dominant states.</p>
</div>

<p>But the genome-wide view says something different:</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>PERMANOVA on gene expression</th><th>R² (variance explained)</th><th>p</th></tr>
  <tr><td>community type alone</td><td>0.020</td><td>0.49</td></tr>
  <tr><td>arm (method) alone</td><td>0.032</td><td>0.09</td></tr>
  <tr><td>route (local vs systemic) alone</td><td>0.022</td><td>0.04</td></tr>
  <tr><td>type + arm together</td><td>0.054</td><td>0.13</td></tr>
</table>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="PCA of gene expression coloured by community type" style="max-width:100%;border:1px solid #ddd;border-radius:6px;margin:.5rem 0">

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>What you're seeing (table + fig9):</strong> the PERMANOVA asks the
coarser question — how much of the <em>overall</em> pattern of gene expression
does each grouping explain (R²), beyond chance? Fig9 is the same PCA as fig7,
recoloured by community type: real separation would mean each colour clumps.</p>
<p><strong>Main finding:</strong> here community type does <em>not</em> win:
R² = 0.020 (p = 0.49) vs arm's 0.032 (p = 0.09) — both tiny, and in fig9 the
colours intermingle (the diverse type just spreads wider, i.e. its members
vary most). So community type points at more individual genes, but explains
less of the genome-wide picture than even the weak method effect.</p>
</div>

<div class="note">
<p><strong>Overall answer: it depends which measure you trust — and that is
the finding.</strong> By the number of individual genes whose expression
differs, community type explains more than method (93 vs 49 genes). But by the
genome-wide variance measure, both explain very little (R² ≈ 0.02–0.03 of a
very noisy phenotype) and method edges out type (0.032 vs 0.020, though
neither is clearly significant). A fair summary: <strong>the microbiome
type is a better pointer to specific host genes than the contraceptive method
is, but neither dominates host gene expression overall</strong>. Two cautions
for your write-up: (1) the two comparisons are not formal statistical tests of
each other — counting significant genes is a heuristic; (2) the diverse type is
nearly synonymous with BV, so even after adjusting for clinical BV status,
some “community type” effect is really “living with a BV-like microbiome”.
The cleanest follow-up: test BV-positive vs BV-negative directly on the genes.</p>
</div>

<h3>How to check this analysis yourself</h3>

<pre><code>Rscript group_project/analysis-cst-genes.R</code></pre>

<p>Sanity checks that would catch a mistake:</p>
<ul>
  <li>Cluster sizes should be 21 / 24 / 48 (crispatus-dom / iners-dom / diverse).</li>
  <li>In fig10, the diverse bar should be full of anaerobes (Gardnerella, Prevotella, Sneathia) while the other two are green Lactobacillus — if the types were defined wrongly, this figure would show it immediately.</li>
  <li>The type × BV table should show 37 of 39 BV-positive people in the diverse type. If that association broke, the whole interpretation would change.</li>
  <li>The gene counts (93 / 49 / 66) should match fig11 — and rerunning changes PERMANOVA p-values slightly (permutation), but not the ordering by R².</li>
  <li>Deliberate robustness check you can try: change <code>k &lt;- 3</code> to <code>k &lt;- 2</code> and rerun — do the broad conclusions survive? (Worth doing for the project; mention what you find under “Choices made”.)</li>
</ul>

<h2>Putting the three questions together</h2>

<p>Each section above answered one question. Here is what they say side by
side, and what they say together.</p>

<table>
  <tr><th>Question</th><th>Strongest evidence</th><th>Verdict</th></tr>
  <tr>
    <td>1. Does the microbiome differ by arm?</td>
    <td>Shannon p = 0.47 (no); arm R² ≈ 0.03, p ≈ 0.1 (weak); 27 species differ ring vs pill</td>
    <td>Only weakly. No difference in diversity; a small species-level tilt towards BV-associated anaerobes in ring/injectable users</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>2. Does the ring differ from systemic methods in gene expression?</td>
    <td>66 of 14,226 genes (0.5%); PCA shift with overlap; both pairwise contrasts agree in direction</td>
    <td>Yes, modestly. Ring tissue leans secretory/inflammatory (<em>BPIFA1</em>, <em>PTGS2</em>); systemic leans squamous maturation (<em>TGM3</em>, <em>KRT1</em>)</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>3. Does community type explain more than method?</td>
    <td>93 genes for type vs 49 for arm — but genome-wide R² 0.020 vs 0.032, both tiny</td>
    <td>Split verdict: type is a better pointer to individual genes; neither explains host expression overall. Type ≈ BV (37 of 39 BV-positive people are the diverse type)</td>
  </tr>
</table>

<div class="reading">
<p><strong>How the graphs fit together:</strong> every figure agrees on one
thing — effects in this dataset are real but small. Fig2 (overlapping boxes)
and fig4 (intermingled colours) say the method barely shapes the microbiome;
fig5 says the little species differences there are, point towards BV-associated
anaerobes in ring/injectable users. Fig7's modest rightward drift of ring
samples is exactly the size you'd predict from those weak microbiome
differences, and fig8 names the genes doing the shifting. Fig10's three clean
microbiome types are by far the sharpest structure in the data — but fig9
shows even they barely separate host expression, only pointing at individual
genes (fig11).</p>
<p><strong>The overall answer to all three questions:</strong> the
<strong>microbiome's state — especially whether it is BV-like — is the main
biological variable in this dataset, and the contraceptive method is a weak
secondary one</strong>. Where the method does leave a fingerprint, it is on
the ring: a slightly more anaerobic microbiome (question 1) and a
secretory/inflammatory host gene programme (question 2), consistent with its
local delivery acting on local tissue. But read question 3's caution before
over-interpreting: the ring's host signal may partly be the tissue responding
to its microbes (<em>BPIFA1</em> is bacteria-induced), and community type is
so entangled with BV that “type explains more than method” is really “BV-like
microbiomes explain more than method”. The honest headline for your project:
<strong>contraceptive method leaves modest, mostly ring-specific marks on both
the microbiome and host expression; BV status is the stronger explanation
everywhere we look</strong>. The obvious next analyses: test BV directly,
and bring in the cytokines to see whether the inflammatory gene programme
shows up in measured inflammation.</p>
<p><strong>One limitation for all three:</strong> this is a cross-sectional
study — one sample per person. Differences between groups are associations;
nothing here proves the method (or the microbiome) <em>caused</em> the
observed changes.</p>
</div>

<h2>Choices made</h2>

<h3>Microbiome vs arm analysis</h3>
<ul>
  <li>Grouping variable <code>arm</code> taken from the metadata, tested against the species table — alternative rejected: defining groups from the counts themselves.</li>
  <li>Alpha diversity measured as Shannon — alternative: observed species count (richness only, ignores evenness).</li>
  <li>Alpha-diversity test: Kruskal–Wallis + pairwise Wilcoxon — alternative: ANOVA on log-transformed values (assumes normality).</li>
  <li>Beta diversity distance: Bray–Curtis on raw counts — alternative: Aitchison distance on CLR-transformed counts (compositional-aware, but harder to explain).</li>
  <li>Ordination: PCoA — alternative: NMDS (no exact axis-variance percentages).</li>
  <li>PERMANOVA with 999 permutations, full model arm + bv + any_sti + batch, plus arm alone — alternative: testing arm adjusted only for batch.</li>
  <li>DESeq2 on raw counts, design ~ rnaseq_batch + bv + arm — alternative: no covariate adjustment (would risk attributing BV effects to the arm).</li>
  <li>Minimal prevalence filter before DESeq2: total reads ≥ 10 per species (keeps 110/220 species) — alternative: no filter (slower, more noise) or a stricter filter (fewer species).</li>
  <li>Significance threshold adjusted p &lt; 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg) — alternative: p &lt; 0.1 to be more sensitive, at the cost of more false positives.</li>
  <li>No samples dropped — alternative: excluding the 3 "intermediate" BV samples (kept, since BV is a covariate, not the grouping variable).</li>
</ul>

<h3>Host gene expression (ring vs systemic)</h3>
<ul>
  <li>Grouping variable <code>route</code> (local = ring vs systemic = pill + injectable) defined from the metadata — alternative: testing the three arms separately without combining.</li>
  <li>Test: DESeq2 on raw gene counts — alternative: limma-voom; alternative rejected: testing on CPM or logged values.</li>
  <li>Design ~ rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti + route — alternative: leaving out <code>any_sti</code> (kept, since STI inflammation could mimic a route effect).</li>
  <li><code>any_sti</code> entered as 0/1 numeric — alternative: factor; equivalent for a two-level variable.</li>
  <li>Gene filter: total reads ≥ 10 — alternative: stricter filter (mean count ≥ 10), which would drop more lowly expressed genes.</li>
  <li>Significance threshold adjusted p &lt; 0.05 across all 14,226 genes (Benjamini–Hochberg) — alternative: a stricter FDR cutoff or requiring a minimum log2FC as well.</li>
  <li>PCA on variance-stabilised values of the 500 most variable genes, for visualisation only — alternative: PCA on log2 CPM; the test itself stays on raw counts.</li>
  <li>Consistency check via a separate arm-in-design model — alternative: forcing arm and route into one design (they are redundant, so this would not be estimable).</li>
  <li>No samples dropped; 19 genes flagged as DESeq2 outliers (Cook's distance) were handled by DESeq2's default — alternative: manual outlier replacement.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Community type vs method analysis</h3>
<ul>
  <li>Community types defined by clustering Bray–Curtis distances with Ward's method, k = 3 chosen by best mean silhouette (0.323) among k = 2–5 — alternative: k = 2 (coarser: Lactobacillus-dominated vs everything else) or rule-based CSTs by dominant species.</li>
  <li>Cluster naming by biology (dominant <em>L. crispatus</em> / <em>L. iners</em> / diverse) — alternative: leaving the neutral names C1–C3, which would be harder to read.</li>
  <li>Gene test: DESeq2 likelihood-ratio test (handles multi-level groupings in one test) — alternative: Wald tests on all pairwise contrasts, then unioning the hits.</li>
  <li>Both LRT models adjust for rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti — alternative: no BV adjustment (rejected: it would mostly re-detect BV, since the diverse type is 77% BV-positive).</li>
  <li>Genome-wide comparison via PERMANOVA on VST values of the 2,000 most variable genes (Euclidean distance) — alternative: PERMANOVA on all genes, or on raw counts (both noisier); VST used only here, never for the per-gene tests.</li>
  <li>“Explains more” reported as two complementary views (gene counts and R²) rather than one — alternative: a single formal non-nested model comparison, which is not standard for DESeq2 group variables.</li>
  <li>No samples dropped; all 14,226 genes tested (the ≥10-read filter kept everything) — alternative: stricter filters, at the cost of losing lowly expressed genes.</li>
</ul>

<h2>How to check this analysis yourself</h2>

<p>Run the script and compare its printed output to the tables above:</p>

<pre><code>Rscript group_project/analysis-microbiome-arm.R</code></pre>

<p>Quick sanity checks that would catch a mistake:</p>
<ul>
  <li>The group sizes should print 28 / 39 / 26 (pill / injectable / ring).</li>
  <li>In fig2, pill's median Shannon (0.90) sits below injectable's (1.74) — but the boxes overlap heavily, matching the non-significant p = 0.47. If a test claimed a big significant difference here, it would be wrong.</li>
  <li>In fig4, the three colours should visibly intermingle — matching arm's small R².</li>
  <li>Rerun <code>perm_arm_alone</code> a second time: the p-value will wobble slightly (≈ 0.09–0.11) because it is permutation-based. That wobble is a feature — it tells you the result is borderline.</li>
  <li>Check the order check line prints <code>Order check passed: 93 samples</code> before any test.</li>
</ul>

<h2>A natural project question</h2>

<p>The question above — “Does the vaginal microbiome (or inflammation) differ
between contraceptive methods?” — is answered in the analysis section above,
with <code>bv</code>, <code>any_sti</code>, and <code>rnaseq_batch</code>
accounted for. Natural extensions for the group project: ask the same question
of the <strong>gene table</strong> (DESeq2 on <code>d$genes</code>), or of the
<strong>cytokines</strong> (inflammation), or make <strong>bv</strong> the main
variable instead of arm.</p>
